title: Before August: A Year of Raising Both the Floor and the Ceiling
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: A third-grade teacher revisits the predictions she made in an earlier post, "Before August," against the actual 2025-26 New York State ELA results, finding her grade level moved sharply against the statewide trend: while state third-grade proficiency fell 11 points to 43%, her school's rose 12 points to 63%, a 23-point swing. She credits three linked changes made across her grade-level team: treating the Wonders literacy curriculum as a flexible tool rather than a script, redefining assessment as ongoing diagnostic information rather than a calendar event, and building a Multi-Tiered System of Supports that pushed struggling readers up while also stretching advanced ones, moving Level 1 students down to 6% and Level 4 students up to 47% in a single year. The piece is explicit that one year of data does not prove the approach will replicate, but frames the results as evidence that strong Tier 1 instruction is a continuous evidentiary process rather than a fixed program.
points: While New York's statewide third-grade ELA proficiency fell 11 points in 2025-26, this teacher's grade level rose 12 points in the same year, a 23-point divergence she attributes to collaborative, data-driven changes to Tier 1 instruction rather than a new curriculum alone.

Her team's MTSS redesign moved students at both ends of the spectrum simultaneously: Level 1 students fell from 13% to 6% of the grade while Level 4 students jumped from 18% to 47%, disproving the assumption that raising the floor requires lowering the ceiling.

Treating the district's Wonders curriculum as a flexible tool rather than a script to follow with fidelity -- prioritizing fluency and vocabulary and letting student performance dictate pacing -- was central to the shift.

The team reframed assessment from a compliance event into a constant diagnostic loop built around two standing questions: what is this student showing us right now, and what will we do differently because of it?
quotes: After a large gain from the 2023-24 year to the 2024-25 year, the third-grade ELA proficiency rate took a drastic drop from 54% in 2024-25 to 43% in 2025-26 - an 11-point decline in a single year.
This year, it jumped to 63%. That's a 12-point increase in a single year while the state fell 11 points - a 23-point swing overall.

In one year, the percentage of third graders performing at the highest tier increased from 18% to 47%. At the same time, our Level 1 percentage dropped from 13% down to 6%. We managed to move students at both ends of the spectrum.

MTSS is often talked about as a system for students who are behind. But that's only half of the job. The students who are already ahead need something from us, too. MTSS should raise the floor without lowering the ceiling.

Instead of worrying about teaching the program with rigid fidelity to the publisher's manual, we began using it as a flexible tool. We put a significant focus on both fluency building and vocabulary knowledge.
That's what a functioning MTSS system should look like: not a system that asks, "Who is below grade level?" but one that asks, "Where is every student right now, and what do they need next?
